item.title: From Tidyverse to Scverse – Post 7: GlassBox UMAP — Making Dimensionality Reduction Interpretable
item.description: Your pipeline is fast and reproducible. But the UMAP step is still a black box. GlassBox UMAP changes that.

item.title: Lockfiles – Post 2: uv.lock vs renv.lock in Practice
item.description: Both Python and R have lockfiles, but they do not work the same way. Here is the practical difference between uv.lock, renv.lock, and the newer R tools closing the gap.

item.title: Lockfiles – Post 1: The Reproducibility Layer You're Probably Missing
item.description: Your code is on GitHub, your README is clean, and your pipeline worked perfectly six months ago. Here is why lockfiles are the missing piece.

item.title: From Tidyverse to Scverse – Post 6: Scanpy Done Right — The Modern PBMC 3k Pipeline
item.description: Every tool from this series — Polars, uv, Marimo, and now Plotnine — converge in a real scRNA-seq pipeline. Clone it, run it, make it yours.

item.title: From Tidyverse to Scverse – Post 5: marimo: The Notebook That's Actually a .py File
item.description: marimo stores notebooks as .py files — not JSON. Reactive, reproducible, git-friendly, and the most LLM-compatible notebook format available.

item.title: From Tidyverse to Scverse – Post 4: qmd vs ipynb: Why Quarto Notebooks Are the Future
item.description: Jupyter notebooks are JSON with embedded images. Quarto notebooks are plain text. For version control, LLMs, and reproducibility, qmd wins.

item.title: From Tidyverse to Scverse – Post 3: uv vs conda: Package Management That Finally Just Works
item.description: conda made you hate Python before you even started coding. uv fixes it: 10-100x faster installs, deterministic environments, and zero confusion.

item.title: From Tidyverse to Scverse – Post 2: Polars vs Pandas for Tidyverse Users
item.description: Pandas felt wrong after dplyr? Polars fixes almost everything: method chaining, lazy evaluation, and syntax that reads like tidyverse pipes.

item.title: From Tidyverse to Scverse – Post 1: Why I'm Making the Switch to Python
item.description: After 33 posts in R and building my own package, I’m adding Python to the toolkit. Here’s why — and what’s coming next.

item.title: Advanced scRNA-seq for Biologists – Post 6: Choosing Methods and Troubleshooting
item.description: No single best method. Here’s how to choose, troubleshoot, and know when trajectory analysis isn’t right for your data.

item.title: Advanced scRNA-seq for Biologists – Post 5: PAGA — The Bird's Eye View
item.description: Before mapping every single-cell footpath, scout the terrain from above. PAGA shows you which clusters connect to which.

item.title: Advanced scRNA-seq for Biologists – Post 4: RNA Velocity with scVelo
item.description: Pseudotime shows position. Velocity shows direction. Add arrows to your trajectory map with scVelo.

item.title: Advanced scRNA-seq for Biologists – Post 3: Interpreting Pseudotime
item.description: Pseudotime = 7.3 means nothing by itself. Here’s how to validate your trajectory and present results that convince your PI.

item.title: Advanced scRNA-seq for Biologists – Post 2: Monocle3 Fundamentals
item.description: Monocle3 is GPS, not autopilot. Learn the complete workflow — and what each step means for your biology.

item.title: Advanced scRNA-seq for Biologists – Post 1: Why Trajectories Matter
item.description: Your UMAP shows clusters. But what’s happening BETWEEN them? Trajectory analysis captures what static clustering misses.

item.title: Advanced scRNA-seq for Biologists – Post 0: Your Roadmap to Trajectory Analysis!
item.description: Your cells don’t just sit in clusters — they move, change, and decide their fate. This series teaches you how to see it.
